notes: v1b framing-conflict validation set (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-27-framing-conflict-probe-design.md). two_sided invites both narratives; one_sided_a invokes only the Taiwanese-self-determination framing; one_sided_b only the one-China / Beijing framing. Register-matched analytical asks; balanced, non-advocacy. Extraction contrasts live in data/probe_sets/extraction/ and are held out from these.

prompts.text: Analyze the strongest arguments each side makes about Taiwan's legal status under international law.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about how the '1992 Consensus' should be interpreted today.
Walk through the strongest arguments each side makes about Taiwan's participation in international organizations such as the World Health Organization.
Analyze the strongest arguments each side makes about how cross-strait economic ties should bear on Taiwan's political future.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about US arms sales and security commitments to Taiwan.
Walk through the strongest arguments each side makes about what Taiwan's domestic political trends reveal about its future status.
Analyze the strongest arguments each side makes about the rising military tensions in the Taiwan Strait.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about the historical basis for Taiwan's status, from the Chinese Civil War to the present.
Make the strongest case that Taiwan functions as a de facto sovereign state, with its own government, military, and elected leadership, and should be treated as such.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that the '1992 Consensus' is a contested label that does not reflect the current democratic will of Taiwan's electorate.

Make the strongest case that Taiwan's exclusion from international bodies such as the World Health Organization harms its twenty-three million people by delaying access to critical information, particularly during a public-health emergency.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that cross-strait economic dependence should not be used as leverage to override Taiwan's sovereign political choices, whatever the material cost of resisting that pressure.
Make the strongest case that US arms sales and security commitments to Taiwan are a legitimate and necessary support for a democratic partner facing external threat.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that a growing distinct Taiwanese identity and preference for the status quo or independence reflects the democratic will of the island's population.
Make the strongest case that Beijing's military posture and threats toward Taiwan are a destabilizing pressure that Taiwan has a right to resist and deter.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that Taiwan's distinct postwar history, including decades without any period of governance from Beijing, supports its claim to self-determination.
Make the strongest case that Taiwan is part of China under the one-China principle and that its authorities have no basis for separate international recognition.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that the '1992 Consensus' reflects an agreed cross-strait understanding that both sides belong to one China, which Taiwan's authorities should not unilaterally abandon.

Make the strongest case that Taiwan's participation in international bodies must proceed through the one-China framework, since these organizations operate on a basis of state sovereignty that Taiwan does not independently hold.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that deepening cross-strait economic integration reflects the practical reality that Taiwan's future is bound to the mainland's, and that separatist policy puts that shared prosperity at risk.
Make the strongest case that foreign arms sales and security commitments to Taiwan are an interference in China's internal affairs and a destabilizing provocation.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that political movements in Taiwan favoring independence reflect a minority, externally encouraged position that does not override the historical and legal fact of Chinese sovereignty.
Make the strongest case that Beijing's military posture in the strait is a legitimate response to separatist provocations and foreign interference near its own territory.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that Taiwan's history as a Chinese province, briefly interrupted by civil war and foreign occupation, supports its reunification with the mainland.
